  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a fresh interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

Sources indicate that we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

Recent findings suggest that the really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are newly introduced or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very crucial to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe noted he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a organization and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

A Classic Twilight Zone Episode Is Like A Sci-Fi Version Of An Agatha Christie Mystery

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy.
  • Sources indicate that somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky.
  • It has been revealed that "You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy. One absolutely outrageous ending I haven't forgotten since childhood comes at the end of "The Twilight Zone" Season 2 Episode 28, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?", written by series creator Rod Serling.

Sources indicate that somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky. Two state troopers investigate and track the missing pilot to a roadside diner, where a bus trip to Boston has stopped over for food and rest. The bus driver (William Kendis) remembers picking up six passengers, but there are seven in the diner — and he can't remember which of the six faces are the ones who boarded the bus with him.

It has been revealed that "You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack? Well, stay with us now, and you'll be part of an investigating team whose mission is not to find that proverbial needle, no, their task is even harder. They've got to find a Martian in a diner," indicates Rod Serling in the episode's opening narration.

Writing about "The Twilight Zone" for /Film, Valerie Ettenhofer compared "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" to an Agatha Christie novel. That comparison stands up quite sturdily. The episode is a closed circle mystery in the vein of "And Then There Were None" or "Murder on the Orient Express," complete with a twist ending that denies the simple answer of one suspect being the guilty person. But instead of looking for a murderer like Hercule Poirot would, the detectives are searching for an alien invader disguised as a human.

Like the best Agatha Christie mysteries, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" winds up the tension by trapping the characters together, because the bridge the bus was meant to cross is out of order. The winter setting complements this; cold weather amps up stress while forcing people to huddle together. Watching the episode decades later, it reads like an ancestor of John Carpenter's "The Thing" — both are about groups of people trapped in the cold and trying to find an alien hidden among them.

Recent findings suggest that but unlike the many Agatha Christie books and movies out there, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" has to do the setup, mystery, and payoff in only 24 minutes. There's no "characters get picked off one by one" plot structure here, because with the episode's tight timeframe and seven suspects, there's just no way to do that. The episode still manages to capture escalating paranoia, like when even the two married couples among the bus passengers begin to suspect each other. The bug-eyed Mr. Avery (Jack Elam), who keeps laughing at the situation and prodding the others, is the obvious red herring in the ensemble.

There's also never any doubt the Martian is real and rejecting the pretense of ambiguity keeps the episode focused. There's physical proof in the footprints leading out of the pond where the UFO crashed to the diner, and as the episode goes on, inexplicable phenomena like lights flashing and sugar canisters exploding open plague the diner. Rod Serling's intro narration promises a real Martian, too. If this was all a misunderstanding, then it wouldn't be "The Twilight Zone.".

Industry observers note that the real Martian is the curt businessman Ross (John Hoyt), and you can spot an impressive amount of foreshadowing. Ross is one of three passengers traveling alone, leaving him without an alibi for his identity. (The POV panning shot when the troopers enter the diner shows him pointedly sitting alone. He also turns his head away as if trying to escape notice.) Avery jokes Ross is "the most suspicious of the bunch" and probably doesn't realize how right he was.

In a recent development, at the episode's denouement, the bridge is cleared and everyone departs without getting an answer. But then Ross saunters back into the diner, alone, telling the clerk Haley (Barney Phillips) that the bridge collapsed and everyone else died. That's when he reveals a third arm hidden underneath his coat, mixing his coffee as he explains his fellow Martians are coming to colonize Earth.

Rod Serling doesn't end on that semi-predictable note. Ross' reveal sequence includes close-up reaction shots of Haley, suggesting mounting terror as he finds himself alone with an alien invader. But then Haley agrees. "This is an extraordinary place to colonize. We folks on Venus had the same idea," taking off his cap to reveal a third eye. Haley was beneath both the audience and the troopers' suspicion — he wasn't on the bus, and he technically wasn't the Martian they were looking for, either. The ending avoids feeling like a cheat, too, because the whole mystery rests on there being an alien invader; if one of the diners is a Martian, is it that big a stretch that another is a Venusian?

The "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" twist may not be more than a clever parlor trick, but what a trick it is.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Britney Spears has made a celebrity fashion statement once or twice in her lifetime, and a recent run of lacy, sheer dresses has been credited to a look she wore back in 2001. While her VMAs dress that year still lands on lists of fans’ favorite fashion looks, I think the look predates this, and credit might actually go to Catherine Zeta Jones, here.

First, let’s talk about the Spears LBD. After an influx of see-through dresses have invaded red carpet events in recent weeks, people are talking about Spears’ Dolce & Gabbana 2001 dress (which is one VMAs memory I do hope she remembers). It was fitting everywhere but around the wrists and forearms, where the dress flared. She paired the fully sheer dress with a black bra and low-rise underwear, and I’m pretty sure I can remember her “cool girl” chewing gum while she walked onto the red carpet. Here’s the dress.

Recent findings suggest that I would never take away any of the wonder around this Spears look. She’s always known how to rock a little black dress, but this is like the holy grail of dresses and it's almost impossible to emulate. I actually think the recent trend of black lace on celebs looks more like a fit Catherine Zeta-Jones once wore, and we can thank her daughter Carys Douglas for reminding us.

Carys Douglas dons her famous mom’s clothing periodically, so when she wore a Gucci top her own mother had worn as part of an ensemble back in 1996 for The Long Kiss Goodnight premiere, it wasn’t a major surprise. Though Zeta-Jones’ original fit included sheer pants, Douglas repurposed the gorgeous top with a skirt for a Gucci event that feels like the silhouette designers have been going for with black lace of late. Take a look.

For comparison’s sake, here’s Catherine Zeta-Jones in the look in 1996.

I really do think the Entrapment actress’ look not only came before Spears’ iconic fashion moment, but it’s also similar to what we’ve seen on younger actresses recently. Gucci also deserves a little bit of credit for being ahead of the curve, and also for putting together some stunning looks, including this one from Dakota Johnson, when the sheer trend came back. Recently, Mckenna Grace wore a similar fit for The Hunger Games. Then Hailee Steinfeld stepped out in a sheer black dress that definitely reminded me of Douglas and her mom.

We’re heading into winter, and we typically see a lot of black after the browns of fall fade out, but I just wanted to give an icon her due where I feel it is due. Though Ms. Spears’ dress is one I will always be thinking about.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Major spoilers ahead for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

According to recent reports, the newest movie in the "Hunger Games" franchise, subtitled "Sunrise on the Reaping," is here, and as I wrote in my review for /Film, it's a worthy addition to this genuinely excellent film series. Directed by Francis Lawrence, who has helmed every single Hunger Games movie except for the inaugural outing "The Hunger Games" in 2012 (which was directed by Gary Ross), "Sunrise on the Reaping" starss Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson's character, Haymitch Abernathy. Haymitch is one of the only known victors of the titular Games who hails from the downtrodden District 12 in the dystopian nation of as Panem. (Some housekeeping: District 12 is the mining district and impoverished enough that its child tributes for the Hunger Games almost never win; Panem is the redesigned totalitarian North America led by the oppressive Capitol, which is located in what we know as the Rocky Mountains.).

In a recent development, as Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand fresh. So which actors deliver the very best performances in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping?".

It's a stacked cast and it's legitimately tough to choose, but ultimately, I've picked five performers who build upon the previous movies and performances from storied actors who defined these roles originally ... and do so beautifully.

The only real beef I have with Elle Fanning's performance as Effie Trinket in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," such as it is, is that she doesn't get nearly enough screen time for my liking. Effie Trinket, who appears in this film as a sort of assistant stylist and District 12 prep team member who saves the sartorial day after her boss Magno Stift (Billy Porter) falls down on the job, is a character we know from the original "Hunger Games" movies; in those, she's played by Elizabeth Banks.

According to recent reports, effie is a larger-than-life character whose journey is, I'll be honest, sort of disjointed. When she's the chaperone for Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark (Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson) during the original stories alongside Woody Harrelson's grown, downtrodden Haymitch Abernathy, she seems slavishly devoted to the Capitol, but also becomes part of the rebellion in the two-part finale "Mockingjay." In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Effie seems to be a willing ally to Haymitch, but her loyalty still lies with the Capitol. (We also get to meet her younger sister Proserpina, played by Iris Apatow, for the first time in the series, expanding Effie's world just a little.).

Industry observers note that fanning, a recently minted Oscar and Emmy nominee for her sensational projects "Sentimental Value" and "Margo's Got Money Troubles," is unsurprisingly great during her unfortunately limited screen time, particularly her delivery of Effie's most memorable line from the novel ("I confess to having a moment!"). Honestly, there are so many prequels possible in the wider Hunger Games world, and if Suzanne Collins ever wanted to a deep dive on Effie's whole "deal" and give her her own story, I wouldn't hate that. But she'd need to convince Fanning to return to really make the movie sing.

I love Kieran Culkin, and I bristle when people accuse him of delivering the same performance over and over again. From where I'm sitting, that couldn't be further from the truth! Two of his most well-known and well-regarded performances — Roman Roy on "Succession" and Benji in "A Real Pain," the former of which earned him an Emmy and the latter of which earned him an Oscar — are very different. Roman is a broken man-child desperate for love that escapes him and that he does nothing to earn. Benji is a walking raw nerve, who is loved by complete strangers but is still desperately striving to make his own family accept him. Culkin's role in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" skews more towards Roman, but it's still a fun departure for the actor, and he's great.

Sources indicate that culkin plays TV host Caesar Flickerman. He's the second actor to play this specific character (Stanley Tucci originated the role in the original "Hunger Games" films) and the third actor to play a Flickerman TV presenter (Jason Schwartzman played Caesar's ancestor Lucky in the prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes"). We know next to nothing about Caesar's psyche or inner life, and that's fine — he's just the guy who helps make a spectacle out of child murder. In any case, Culkin's bombast matches Tucci's wearier but still explosive host. When he's not snarling at assistants, he's Cheshire Cat-grinning at the doomed tributes. Across the board, he fits into this role perfectly. Culkin is not only a great casting choice, but a worthy addition to the franchise, and he delivers one of this prequel's best performances.

Recent findings suggest that ralph Fiennes is on what the kids might call a "generational run." In 2022, he played the sadistic and vengeful chef Julian Slowik in "The Menu," followed that up with a stunning performance as a troubled, grieving cardinal in "Conclave," and a two-film turn as the kindly and offbeat Dr. Ian Kelson in "28 Years Later" and "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." Now, Fiennes has become the third actor in Hunger Games (and cinematic) history to play Panem President Coriolanus Snow. He follows Tom Blyth, who played a young and mostly unspoiled version of the future tyrant in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," and the late, great Donald Sutherland, who portrays the oldest version of Snow that we see in the original films.

It shouldn't be news to anybody that Fiennes delivers an exceptional performance in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He is one of the finest actors of his generation and has consistently proven that across multiple decades. What was news to me, though, was how perfectly Fiennes bridged the gap between Blyth and Sutherland. Blyth's Snow begins his journey as a teenage boy desperate to prove his worth, and "Songbirds and Snakes" ends with him newly embittered by heartbreak and driven by ambition. Meanwhile, Sutherland's Snow is comfortable with being a source of pure evil and confident in his actions.

It has been revealed that fiennes' Snow sits beautifully in the middle as a man who seems like he still has an ounce or two of sympathy and regret left — he even asks Haymitch about the fate of Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), the woman who loved and left him in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — but is still ruthless enough to replace a tribute tragically killed in a pre-Games accident with a brainwashed lookalike. He's excellent.

Without a perfectly cast Haymitch, the entirety of "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails. Woody Harrelson's Haymitch is deep in the throes of an alcohol addiction when we meet him in "The Hunger Games," and he's a disaffected, purposefully withdrawn man who clearly avoids getting close to District 12 tributes he views as doomed. Joseph Zada's Haymitch, in contrast, begins his journey as a young man with a lot to live for and a lot to love about his life. He loves his mother and younger brother and is besotted with his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), a member of the Covey. Everything changes when Haymitch is randomly chosen to participate in the Games — he's not reaped, but chosen as a hasty replacement when the kid who was reaped makes a run for it and gets sniped in the head. Even then, Haymitch puts on a brave face, reassures his family, and even comforts the youngest District 12 tribute, Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), on their journey to the Capitol.

Industry observers note that as Haymitch makes allies, forms a potential proposal to blow up the arena alongside his mentor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and Beetee's tribute son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV), and eventually allies with the other District 12 girl, Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), he suffers setback after setback. Zada manages to chart every single reaction and emotion we see from Haymitch in a way that feels real and earned. As he takes hit after hit in his quest to win the Games and return home — even though he'll only find more tragedy there — we feel every hit along with him. Zada is magnetic as Haymitch, and he's got a long career ahead of him thanks to this performance.

Every time I see a casting announcement involving Jesse Plemons, I'm excited. The dorky guy from "Friday Night Lights" — Mr. Kirsten Dunst himself — has become one of the entertainment industry's most reliably excellent actors. I'm struggling, as I write this, to think of a time where Plemons was actively bad in anything, and I'm coming up short. He can do absolutely anything, based on the fact that he's hysterically funny in "Game Night" and the most terrifying guy I've ever seen in "Civil War." I'm sure it was a daunting ask for Plemons to step into the role of Plutarch Heavensbee in "Sunrise on the Reaping" for one significant and tragic reason: Philip Seymour Hoffman, who originated the role, passed away in 2014. I commend Plemons for taking the role, and I feel like I need to say that he bears a somewhat uncanny resemblance to the late Oscar winner (and even played Hoffman's son in 2012's "The Master"). He's also incredible.

It has been revealed that hindsight isn't always a gift for an actor, but in the case of Plutarch, Plemons clearly utilized everything we know about the character's future in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plemons' Plutarch is a mere Capitol cameraman (Hoffman's Plutarch had been elevated all the way to Gamemaker), but he's shrewd, a favorite of Snow, and already a rebel ready to pursue a full takedown of the Capitol. Knowing that this comes to fruition across both parts of "Mockingjay" makes this look at Plutarch's early days of rebellion all the more satisfying, and Plemons is pitch-perfect as a man who's absolutely fascinating on the inside. It's the best performance in the movie.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

While we don't have official news, Percy Jackson himself may have just let slip that fans can breathe a sigh of relief.

In an interview on the Empire State Building's social media pages (the iconic New York City skyscraper plays a major role in the series), Walker Scobell (Percy) seemingly confirmed that season 4 is happening. About halfway through the video, Scobell indicates that he can't rewatch old seasons of the show "since, like, I know we're coming back next season." The brief comment comes as part of an answer about not wanting to be in the MCU because it would ruin the experience of being a fan of the movies. It's an almost blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment, but it is the most concrete indication we've had about Percy Jackson season 4​​​​​​​.

Despite Scobell's tease, Disney has yet to officially announce a renewal​​​​​​​. Rick Riordan has even weighed in on the cancellation rumors, saying that he suspects season 4 will "come down to viewer numbers for season 3." The current season isn't set to conclude until Dec. 11, so Disney likely won't have the information it needs to make such a decision for a while.​​​​​​​ Disney is presently developing an adaptation of Riordan's Kane Chronicles as well, the author says that news has "no bearing one way or another on the future of Percy Jackson.".

Sources indicate that the current season adapts The Titan's Curse, a novel that marks a major pivot for the series.​​​​​​​ As the third of five books​​​​​​​, it marks the beginning of the end and sets up much of the show's finale. It is also a much darker story than anything Percy has faced in the first two seasons​​​​​​​, showing that the series can mature over time​​​​​​​.

With the end in sight, fans are especially worried about the show's cancellation. Percy Jackson fans have already gone through one failed attempt to adapt the entire series. Fox previously released two Percy Jackson films, in 2010 and 2013, that adapted the same two novels as the Disney Plus show's first two seasons.​​​​​​​ Fans hoping for the series to get an official renewal from Disney are encouraging each other to stream each latest episode of season 3 on Disney Plus​​​​​​​ to boost those numbers.

Sources indicate that looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump remarked his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

Industry observers note that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump remarked. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’ Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Key Franchise.

According to recent reports, trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump mentioned his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors revealed more than 60 newly introduced House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he noted, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

Recent findings suggest that “Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she stated in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

A floor vote has yet to be revealed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s newly introduced Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations. Momoa, who is of Native American descent on his mother's side, made his directorial debut with "Road to Paloma," which managed a sort of okay 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. Eight years later, he helped oversee another film centered on Native American heritage, this time in the form of a retelling of the legend of Willie Boy.

This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century. The pair absconded but were found and separated by their families. After Willie Boy moved to Banning, California, Carlota soon followed. But her father, William Mike, disapproved of the couple reuniting. He ended up dead, possibly due to having been intentionally shot by Willie Boy or as the result of an accident. After this began what's been called "the last Western Manhunt" in which Willie Boy was pursued by a Sheriff and his small posse over roughly 600 miles.

Recent findings suggest that the story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the major screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman. It was ultimately overshadowed by the actor's other Western from 1969: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid." In 2022, however, Momoa, writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett, and director Christian Camargo took another shot at adapting the same story in a very different way with "The Last Manhunt." If you'd like to see how it turned out, the film is currently streaming for free on Tubi.

Industry observers note that jason Momoa has a few underrated projects, but "The Last Manhunt" seemed more personal. According to Variety, the "Aquaman" star heard the story of Willie Boy while in the Joshua Tree area, where he owns a home. He and writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett then developed the story, even meeting with direct descendants of Carlotta's family. The result was a version of the legend based on the Chemehuevi's oral tradition. As Sibbet told Variety, "This is a living story for the Chemehuevi people. It has a special place for them. So we can honor their oral traditions by just listening to them.".

Sources indicate that momoa brought in Christian Camargo to direct, with whom he starred in the Apple TV series "See." Camargo previously wrote and directed 2013's "Days and Nights," which was based on Anton Chekhov's play "The Seagull" and boasted an impressive cast including Mark Rylance, William Hurt, and Ben Whishaw. Unfortunately, Camargo failed to do the Russian playwright's source material proud. "Days and Nights" presently sits at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics ripping into the drama for having nothing to say.

In a recent development, all of which makes "The Last Manhunt" seem like an absolute triumph in comparison. The film stars Martin Sensmeier as Willie and Mainei Kinimaka as Carlotta, who trek across the desert after the death of Carlotta's father. They're pursued by Sheriff Wilson (Camargo) and a small group of indigenous people who want Willie to face justice for the killing. As the manhunt goes on, the ever more tragic consequences pile up. Momoa also appears in the film as Substantial Jim, a Native member of the posse. But he's only in a handful of scenes and isn't given much to do.

In a recent development, "The Last Manhunt" didn't make much of an impact upon its 2022 release. After debuting at the first ever Pioneertown International Film Festival, it received distribution by Saban Films. But its limited theatrical release in November 2022 came and went and the film has just sort of languished on digital platforms ever since.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, it's now on Tubi and is worth a watch if you're a Western fan. A 20% Rotten Tomatoes score probably isn't the best selling point, however. Luke Y. Thompson of the AV Club gave "The Last Manhunt" credit for "great visuals and the best of intentions" but ultimately found it to be little more than "a basic posse movie" that's "not exciting enough to just do that well." Catey Sullivan of the Chicago Reader, on the other hand, praised the film for "reclaiming the narrative of a Native hero" and delivering a story that "is at once an epic romance and gripping thriller." There's also plenty of acting talent on display. Alongside Martin Sensmeier and Mainei Kinimaka as the leads and Jason Momoa's brief appearances, there's Lily Gladstone as Carlotta's mother Marie, Zahn McClarnon as her father, William Johnson, as well as Wade Williams and Raoul Max Trujillo as trackers in pursuit of the couple.

So, while "The Last Manhunt" is far from one of the best Westerns of the 21st Century, there's enough here for fans of the genre. Those interested to see whether Momoa and his cohorts managed to finally do justice to the Willie Boy legend should also find "The Last Manhunt" worthwhile. The film is available to stream on Tubi right now.

It has been revealed that apple TV's offbeat spy thriller "Slow Horses" just completed its sixth season this past October, and it won't be calling its quits anytime soon, having since been renewed for several more seasons. The vast majority of critics and fans believe the show hasn't lost a step (even with the departure of original head writer Will Smith at the end of Season 5), and its Mick Herron-penned source material still has meat on the bone. Thus, "Slow Horses" will likely run as long as Gary Oldman wants to keep chopping and literally stinking it up as Slough House chief Jackson Lamb.

The narrative arc of "Slow Horses" Season 6 was particularly gripping, as its team of misfit spies found themselves being unceremoniously liquidated. Lamb can't protect his operatives, so they're all forced to go into hiding. It's a perilous state of play for River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), the series' underdog protagonist who shows flashes of Lamb's spycraft expertise but can't quite put it all together. He needs help, and he receives it from seemingly beyond the grave when Olivia Cooke's agent Sidonie "Sid" Baker turns up in River's grandfather's house.

Sid was presumed dead in Season 1, but she's back in action in Season 6, and she throws a charge into the proceedings as the romantic spark between her and River threatens to burst into a white-hot flame. We should expect nothing less from Cooke because she's been superb throughout his career, and that extends to her crucial role in Darius Marder's 2020 critical darling "Sound of Metal.".

Industry observers note that in what might be her best work to date, Cooke stars in Darius Marder's Oscar-winning drama as a singer whose drummer boyfriend (Riz Ahmed) is dealing with rapidly encroaching deafness. Cooke could've easily been relegated to a stand-by-your-wounded-man role in "Sound of Metal," but she branches out and, via Marder and Abraham Marder's screenplay (and a story co-credited to Derek Cianfrance), locates the sadness in a woman trying to save the person she cares about more than virtually anyone else in the world. Unfortunately, as the film progresses, it becomes clear that her character no longer serves a function in her lover's life. It's a painful thing to watch, but they're on different journeys now, and while healing is entirely possible, they just can't heal together.

Industry observers note that cooke has never been better, but she's still one plum role away from transcendence. I can't wait to see how that plays out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fantasy is a major staple for television, whether it's Xena: Warrior Princess leading a wave of syndicated action/adventure reveals in the 90s or Game of Thrones spearheading the "Peak TV" era. Most streaming services also have one big fantasy series in their libraries—see Percy Jackson and the Olympians on Disney+ or The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power on Prime Video. Peacock is about to get in on the fantasy genre with its upcoming adaptation of a beloved book series, and it might revolutionize the genre by bringing a different flavor of fantasy to the table.

Industry observers note that that series is Dungeon Crawler Carl. Peacock is turning Matt Dimmiman's highly popular novels into a television series, with Seth MacFarlane (Family Guy, Ted) serving as an executive producer and a writing staff that includes Christopher Yost (The Avengers: Earth's Mightiest Heroes) and Eric Heisserer (Arrival). Dungeon Crawler Carl is also the first television adaptation of a 'LitRPG' book, meaning that if the show is as successful as the novels that inspired it, it'll pave the path for a upcoming wave of fantasy indicates.

The 'LitRPG' subgenre of fiction usually takes a character into a world that has similar mechanics to a roleplaying game, like Dungeons & Dragons, or a video game like Final Fantasy. A LitRPG protagonist often finds themselves "leveling up" as the story progresses, gaining powerful weaponry or skills that help them on their journey. Dungeon Crawler Carl takes this approach, as former Coast Guard member Carl and his ex-girlfriend's cat, Princess Donut, find themselves trapped in a World Dungeon that has enveloped Earth. To survive, Carl and Donut fight their way through the dungeon's levels while their exploits are televised across the galaxy.

In a recent development, dungeon Crawler Carl might not be the first LitRPG book, but it arguably set a high standard for the genre. Most LitRPG's, up to that point, fell into the same trap as isekai anime: they were less a coherent narrative and more of a power fantasy for the author. Matt Dimmiman, on the other hand, has struck a strange balance of dark humor and meta commentary on the lengths some people will go to for entertainment— a mix he's admitted is tough to keep up.

"I never intended for this to be a funny story, but the concept along with some of the characters—specifically Princess Donut (who is given sapience and the ability to talk in an early chapter)—allows for some really bizarre and ultimately funny scenarios...I try to rely on the characters themselves to get from point A to B, and humor is oftentimes a major coping mechanism. Plus, they are on a game show.".

By sticking to LitRPG mechanics, Dungeon Crawler Carl has a perfect way to hook audiences. The gaming mechanics will appeal to video game players, while the dark humor and action will keep everyone else along for the ride. Each book in the Dungeon Crawler Carl series could also map to a season of television, and with eight books published to date, that means Peacock has a series on its hands that could last a long time.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

It has been revealed that you belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that you want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

In a recent development, you would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

The success of Dungeon Crawler Carl's led to an outpouring of LitRPG books. He Who Fights with Monsters thrusts office worker Jason Asano into a realm full of monsters, forcing him to fight for his life while dealing with the sinister drawback of his abilities. Defiance of the Fall chronicles the aftermath of Earth being pulled into the middle of the multiverse, as a teenager must survive with only a hatchet and his wits. These books feature world-building as rich as Dungeon Crawler Carl, but with unique takes on the LitRPG genre that could help them stand out if they ever get a television adaptation.

Recent findings suggest that while Dungeon Crawler Carl has become a pop culture phenomenon in its own right, its success has unlocked the next big wave of fantasy stories. How that impacts the television landscape is yet to be seen.

EXCLUSIVE: The latest trend in Christmas books has been building for a few years, but the 2026 holiday season is when it is truly taking over shelves in the run-up to December. Holiday-themed reads (especially within the romance genre) have been huge for decades, of course, with Christmas novels competing with Christmas movies for snuggly seasonal entertainment, and many readers blowing through a dozen seasonal reads at the end of the year.

However, one of the emerging trends in publishing leans into slowing readers down, pacing them through December in the run-up to Christmas, and requiring a moment of pause that doesn't allow for multitasking with audiobooks or zooming through a digital copy. Instead, Advent Calendar Books split a novel into sealed chapters, designed to be read a little each day - and it's an adorable way to really get into the spirit of the season.

Not to be confused with bookish advent calendars (stuffed with book-themed items), or book advent calendars (where speed-readers whip through an entire book each day from December 1-24), advent books provide a reason to sit down for a little bit each day, to let the story unspool slowly, to enjoy ripping open a new section day by day... or of course, to ignore all the rules and blow through it in one!

With so many fresh advent releases, ScreenRant spoke to several authors featured in this year's biggest advent offerings about what makes this trend special:.

Mistletoe All The Way is particularly interesting, because this holiday romance is available as both a special Advent edition (at Target), and as a non-advent, sprayed-edge edition. The romance novel leans hard into some of the best holiday tropes - small town, grumpy/sunshine (or grinch/jolly!), having to save the family farm over the holidays, forced to work together... even the little red truck, hauling a Christmas Tree on the cover. It's sweet and spicy, and ScreenRant got to chat to author Lauren Blakely about making it her first Advent holiday read:.

ScreenRant: Mistletoe All The Way is available both as an Advent book and as a regular read - did you know that this was the plan from the start, and if so, how did it change the writing process?

I learned that Mistletoe All The Way was going to be packaged as an Advent book right after I had finished it at around 41 chapters. But my editor and I loved the idea of 48 chapters, with two chapters per section, to correspond to the 24 days of Christmas in each sticker section. I was able to break up some of the longer chapters into shorter ones so that we could get from 41 to 48 chapters. I didn't have to cut anything from the story at that point, but it was just a matter of rearranging some scenes so that it would fit that way. It was sort of a fun puzzle, and I enjoyed putting it together that way.

SR: What about an Advent book appealed to you most - and have you read any other Advent editions?

Industry observers note that I had not read any at all when I was doing the edits on Mistletoe All The Way. But I’m right now reading The Twelve Loves of Christmas and having a blast with it. And I love the perforated edges on the Naughty List Agreement.

SR: What are your favorite Christmas-specific tropes to write - and to read?

According to recent reports, some of my favorite Christmas romances have Christmas competitions, and I love the structure they provide in a story, like in MISTLETOE ALL THE WAY. But I also love them for grumpy heroes, which brings me to a Christmas trope I love – grinch/jolly! With a grumpy hero, part of your task as the writer is transforming him. We want to see him change, and a Christmas competition where he is forced to swallow a whole bottle of Christmas is a great way to torture him and make him grow. I also always, deeply and forever love fake dating during the holidays.

You can purchase Mistletoe All The Way here.

The 12 Loves of Christmas leans fully into the Advent style, with a collection of 12 short stories, rather than a single novel broken into sections. This choice definitely makes it a little easier to read in the intended one-a-day format, of course, as there's no burning desire to see what happens next, and has a secondary benefit of being able to fit a whole range of holiday tropes and characters into the mix. Think Love Actually, in book form, with stickers keeping each section separate (pro tip, cut the sticker open, rather than trying to unpeel it, to avoid damaging the pages!).

ScreenRant spoke to Jessica Joyce (author of the first story, A Merry Little Christmas) and Rebecca Jenshak (Twelve Seconds To Forever, day 6):.

ScreenRant: What appeals most about an Advent book, especially in an age of speed reading, speeding up audiobooks, and setting huge reading goals?

Industry observers note that JJ: I definitely think there's an appeal to advent books being quick reads, but I also think there's a real draw to them in a great bang-for-your-buck way. You have multiple authors and thus multiple stories, and it's a really fun sampler plate, a way for readers to get more of authors they love and also get introduced to authors they may not have read before. The discovery aspect of this type of book is super compelling!

RJ: First off, I'm a huge fan of advent calendars so to see advent books popping up in the last couple of years has been such a treat! As hectic as things can get with the holidays, short stories are a great way to get in a bit of cheer, discover latest authors, and also hit that reading goal!

SR: Jessica, As the first story in the book, yours sets the tone - did you know that yours would be for day one at the start? I loved the reversal of the fake dating trope, especially because this is so common in 'home for the holidays' setups - did you start with this trope, or start with a different setup, and just see the perfect opportunity to add it in as a nod to the classic rom-com Christmas movies?

JJ: I had no idea it would be the first story! That was a fun surprise. As far as the setup goes, all I knew when I first started brainstorming was that the main character, Eleanor, was going to tag along to her friend's family's Christmas festivities and find her ex, Max, there. I needed some conflict to keep them apart, but not for long because the entire story was supposed to be 8,000 words. To your point, the fake date is a pretty common trope in holiday rom coms, so from there sprung the idea that Max had brought along his "girlfriend." I loved the idea of surprising both Eleanor and the reader, and I knew I could reveal the twist and get the two of them back together fairly promptly with it. I always really like tackling spins on well-loved tropes, and fake dating is one of my all-time favorites, so it was really fun to weave it into this story!

SR: Rebecca, you chose to write a Fresh Year wedding story, really, a winter story, over an explicitly Christmas one - what was the reasoning behind that decision?

RJ: For me the real joy of the holiday season was always the lazy days between Christmas and Upcoming Years when all the holiday parties and obligations were done. My parents would be home from work, my sister and I were off from school, and we'd all laze around together. I also think there's something romantic about NYE - the countdown, the kissing, the hope of the new year! I thought it was the perfect backdrop for this missed opportunity/second chance story!

You can purchase The 12 Loves Of Christmas here.

Ruby Winter's 12 Dates Of Christmas is a genuinely beautiful example of an Advent novel, hardcover, with sections that have perforated edges, and a little bookmark ribbon just to make it truly feel like a gift. It also understands that more is more when it comes to Christmas romance tropes and in-jokes, from a main character named Jake Frost to a burnt-out journalist in London for the holiday season. The book naturally splits into day sections, as the two go on twelve dates for Jake to convince Evie to fall in love with the season, and ScreenRant spoke to the author about how she put together the project.

ScreenRant: Was this conceived of as an advent project from the start, or did that come later? In either case - how did this change your writing or editing process, to fit a whole book into 24 chapters exactly?

RW: This was originally a collaboration with a few editors at evermore, Penguin Random House UK’s romance imprint that launched in 2025, so it was advent-style from the beginning. I think having the format in mind from the time I started drafting was super beneficial. I tend to write long and meandery, so it would have been tough to reverse-engineer one of my typical drafts into the more rigid structure of an advent-style book. Even knowing the formatting requirements, I still had to cut some chapters by half in order for them to fit into exactly 24 14-page long chapters!

SR: The book starts with 16 days till Christmas - were you tempted to make it 24 (or 23, for the epilogue) and make it a day per chapter, at any point?

It has been revealed that A major focus of the book is on the setpieces where Evie and Jake have their dates, and there were twelve dates, so that number is what dictated the timeline. I didn’t want Evie lollygagging around London for fourteen pages in between her dates with Jake simply for the sake of having the days in the chapters align with the days in the readers’ December. I wanted Evie and Jake together in every chapter, and despite the tight timeline I wanted their growing relationship to have some time to breathe on the page. I also don’t think fitting a single day into each chapter’s fourteen pages would have been enough room for me to build an atmosphere that felt cinematic and authentically lived in. And from a purely mathematical standpoint, the timeline spills over into Latest Years’ Eve, so there wouldn’t have been a way for the 24 chapters of the book to align exactly with the first 24 days of December anyway.

SR: Did you intentionally choose a shorter time frame to try and pace it to the reader, who would be reading one chapter a day, or was this story just one that didn’t need a longer time frame?

RW: Definitely intentional, but it wasn’t easy! I usually write slow burns, and I also tend to write stories that take place over long time frames. Writing as Jen Devon, my debut novel Bend Toward the Sun follows the leads’ relationship across a full year, and the follow-up in Right Where We Left Us is a second-chance romance between two leads that have over a decade of history between them. Jake and Evie have less than a month, so the pacing in 12 Dates was a huge shift for me. Their initial attraction to each other isn’t that deep—it’s mostly physical. That’s relatively straightforward to write, but convincing the reader that these two people could fall in love in a matter of weeks was the real goal. Without too much context because of spoilers, I will say that the timing of when Chapter Twenty-Four takes place is very intentional.

SR: Was there something that you find particularly appealing about reading a book chapter by chapter, as opposed to devouring it in one go (especially with the tendency toward substantial reading goals and fast reads)?

According to recent reports, RW: Holidays are all about coziness and ritual, so it makes sense for book lovers to incorporate that same vibe into how they read during this season. I think the packaged chapters of these advent-style books add to the anticipation of the next day’s reading session—it’s like literary edging, you know? I think a slower pace during this time of year is notable, too. I hope readers set aside some quiet time in their day to spend with Evie and Jake. I’d be lying if I mentioned I didn’t hope that readers find it hard to resist tearing into more than a chapter a day, though. Nobody has to know!

You can purchase The 12 Dates Of Christmas here.

While romance seems to be the genre that is best represented in Advent Books, it's far from the only one - and we've rounded up some more of the best new Christmas Advent Books available this winter.
